content: Influenza vaccination is widely recommended for individuals with asthma in many countries, as observational studies have suggested a link between influenza infection and asthma exacerbations. However, there is concern that influenza vaccination itself may induce wheezing or negatively impact pulmonary function. While some reviews have concluded that influenza vaccination does not provide clear benefits for asthmatic patients, these conclusions were not based on a systematic review of the available literature. The purpose of this review was to evaluate both the efficacy and safety of influenza vaccination in children and adults with asthma. The review included randomized trials involving individuals with asthma aged over two years, while excluding studies that involved patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The search for relevant studies was conducted through the Cochrane Airways Group trials register, and the most recent search was completed in November 2012. Data extraction and quality assessment of the included trials were performed independently by two reviewers, and study authors were contacted when additional information was required. A total of nine trials were included in the initial version of this review, with nine additional trials incorporated in subsequent updates. The studies included a diverse range of participants, settings, and types of influenza vaccines. Data were pooled from studies that used similar vaccine types. Protective effects of inactivated influenza vaccine during the influenza season: One parallel-group trial involving 696 children assessed the protective effects of inactivated influenza vaccination. The results showed no significant reduction in the number, duration, or severity of influenza-related asthma exacerbations. Forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) did not differ significantly between vaccinated and unvaccinated children, although vaccinated children demonstrated better symptom scores during weeks with confirmed influenza. Two additional parallel-group trials in adults did not contribute data to these outcomes due to very low levels of confirmed influenza infection. Adverse effects of inactivated influenza vaccine in the first two weeks following vaccination: Two crossover trials, which included 1526 adults and 712 children (aged over three years) with asthma, compared the inactivated trivalent split-virus influenza vaccine to a placebo injection. These trials found no clinically significant increase in asthma exacerbations within the two weeks following vaccination (risk difference 0.014; 95% confidence interval -0.010 to 0.037). However, there was notable variability in the findings of two trials involving 1104 adults regarding asthma exacerbations within the first three days after vaccination with split-virus or surface-antigen inactivated vaccines. No significant differences were observed in healthcare utilization, days off school, symptom-free days, mean lung function, or medication usage. Effects of live attenuated (intranasal) influenza vaccination: Two small studies, involving 17 adults and 48 children, compared live attenuated cold recombinant influenza vaccine to a placebo. These studies found no significant differences in asthma exacerbations or lung function measures following vaccination. Additionally, one study involving 2229 children (aged over six years) compared live attenuated intranasal vaccine to trivalent inactivated intramuscular vaccine and found no significant differences in asthma exacerbations between the two groups. Authors' conclusions: There remains uncertainty regarding the extent to which influenza vaccination protects against asthma exacerbations triggered by influenza infection. Evidence from more recent randomized trials of inactivated split-virus influenza vaccines suggests that there is no significant increase in asthma exacerbations immediately following vaccination in adults or children over three years of age. However, concerns about increased wheezing and hospital admissions in infants receiving live intranasal vaccination could not be addressed by this review.
